plain_definition: A free 3-day summer event at the university where new disabled students stay in student rooms and meet friends before courses start in September.
The full name of the STAR programme; 'residential' means you stay overnight in student rooms on campus.
A student who has applied to the university and received an acceptance letter or offer to study here, but has not yet officially started classes.
A friendly current university student whose job is to guide new students, answer questions, lead campus walks, and help you settle in.
The university department that arranges special help for students who have medical conditions, disabilities, or learning difficulties like dyslexia.
An official written plan listing the extra help you need for classes and exams (such as extra exam time or permission to record lectures).
Fair changes made to teaching, exams, or buildings to make sure disabled students have the same chances as everyone else.
A UK government grant (money that you do not need to pay back) to buy special study equipment, software, or tutoring for your course.
An informal meeting with an expert who asks how your condition affects your studying, in order to recommend helpful software and equipment.
Apartment buildings owned by the university where students rent individual study bedrooms and share a kitchen with other students.
A private bedroom that has its own private bathroom (toilet, shower, and sink) inside the bedroom.
A specially designed bedroom with wider doors, lowered switches, and a wheel-in shower for students who use wheelchairs or mobility aids.
The main welcome desk in the Student Centre where you can ask any general questions about university life, fees, or your student card.
An easy website and phone app used at UCLan to book appointments with tutors, disability advisers, and wellbeing counselors.
A free university service that teaches you how to write academic essays, read research papers, and do referencing correctly.
A confidential team of trained staff offering free support when you feel anxious, stressed, lonely, or homesick.
The university's online course website where teachers post lecture slides, readings, homework tasks, and assignment submission links.
An online system where you submit your essays to check that you have quoted and referenced your research sources properly.
The first week before classes start in September, full of fun social events, campus tours, and meeting new classmates.
A big market-style event during Welcome Week where you can join student sports clubs, social societies, and collect free gifts.
A university lecturer assigned to you who meets with you regularly throughout your degree to check on your academic progress and give guidance.
Practice homework or presentations where you receive teacher feedback to help you improve, but the score does not count towards your final grade.
Final graded exams, essays, or projects that count directly towards your official course mark and university degree.
The official process of confirming your identity, enrolling onto your classes, and getting your official university student ID card.
A student who has spent time living in foster care or in children's residential homes before coming to university.
A student who has no contact with, or financial/emotional support from, their parents or family.
A professional support worker who assists a disabled student with daily personal care, mobility, or communication needs.
A special fire alarm system that flashes bright lights and vibrates a pocket receiver to warn students who cannot hear standard alarms.
A learning difference such as dyslexia (trouble with reading/spelling) or dyspraxia (trouble with physical coordination) that does not affect general intelligence.
A time when you can visit an office or service to talk with an advisor without booking an appointment in advance.
